utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, Exhibit D35 is an order dated the 6th of July, 1994, issued by Minister of Defence Susak. Let me ask you first if you were familiar with this order at the time or about the time it was issued?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the order, but the genesis of the order. That's to say the underlying reasons for its issuance.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can all the extra microphones be switched off, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And why was that order issued?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of the town of Dubrovnik, the 5th Company of the 72nd Military Police Battalion was active, which in accordance with Article 9, according to the daily operational command, was subordinated to the commander of the southern front. As part of the company, there were military police platoons. The Croatian -- the reserve brigades of the Croatian army, which were part of the forces deployed in the southern front. There came about a situation where the commander of the southern front ordered, prompted by the activities of one of the members of these military police platoons, I will not say of which reserve brigade they were a member, the commander asked that the commander who was arrested for breach of discipline, be released from the detention premises and not to report to the superior command which was, in this case, the 72nd Military Police Battalion. When the commander of that platoon and the commander of the company of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, refused to act upon the oral order of the commander of the southern front, he issued an order where he abolished or disbanded the platoon and turned into a regular infantry platoon. Another infantry platoon of that brigade was in turn transformed into a military police platoon. The members of the -- of what was formally the military police platoon were ordered to hand over all the weapons they had, the communications devices, et cetera, which was in violations of the rules governing the military police and it was also -- it also constituted the overstepping of the powers granted under Article 9 to the military personnel over the military police. There were attempts to resolve this in contact with the commander of the 72nd Battalion and the commander of the southern front. Since it was impossible to resolve it at that level, the commander of the 72nd Battalion reported on this to the administration of the military police. I personally spoke to the commander of the southern front to repeal that order. The individual concerned refused to do that. And I informed the ministry thereof. The minister, in turn, issued a new order, in the preamble of which it was highlight that the order was issued on the basis of the minister's powers granted under the law, and the Law on Defence, in order to remove any matters that may remain vague in the line of command over the military police, acting upon the information received from the command of the 72nd Military Police Battalion and about the conduct of the platoons that were members of that 72nd Battalion, in the southern front. The order was quite specific in its terms, and in Article 10, or item 10, of that particular order, the ministry vacated all the orders that came down along the line of command to the military police units and which were issued contrary to the provisions of the legislation in this particular order. That's the genesis of the order, which I might -- I have to say was quite unusual. However, this was the only means of resolving the incident. I have say that the commander of the southern front fully adhered to the order. It was fully implemented, and the military policemen involved were again posted to the positions and in -- and charged with the duties that they had been carrying out previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, at the beginning of your answer, you indicated that the military police battalion was active in a certain area which in accordance with Article 9, according to the daily operational command was subordinated to the commander of the southern front. When you say "according to the daily operational command," is that the same thing or different from that what is stated in Article 9 while performing their regular military police tasks, military police units are subordinate to the commander of the Military District, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain this because in your question you said that it had to do with the commander of the battalion. This was the situation. The 72nd Military Police Battalion at the time, and we're referring to 1994, had, as its area of operation, the area stretching from the island of Pag all the way to Dubrovnik. It was active in the area of the Split Military District and that of the southern front. The southern front was the area stretching from Ploce to Dubrovnik and it was in this area --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt for a second. And the question seems as if it was confusing. It wasn't interested so much in the geographic area of responsibility as I was in the terminology. And as I indicated, at the beginning of your question, you used the term: "According to the daily operational command was subordinated to the commander of the southern front?" And I just wanted to know if that term "daily operational command was contemplated the same subordination or anything different from the language of Article 9 which states: "While performing their regular military police tasks, military police units are subordinate to the commander of the Military District and the other officials listed."

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the sake of precision, in my answer, I wanted to highlight that the 5th Company of the 72nd Battalion had as its area of responsibility the southern front, which was not the area falling under the Split Military District. Whereas other companies of the 72nd Battalion were covering the area that was the AOR of the Split Military District. Now to answer your question. The daily operational command had to do with the carrying out of the -- all daily tasks of the military police referred to in Article 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I want to move on to another question, but I wanted to ask you if the circumstances that gave rise to the 1994 order about Minister of Defence Susak, that is, the existence of platoons attached to brigades whether that situation continued to exist in 1995 at the time of Operation Storm. At that point, were military police platoons still attached to brigades?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question with precision, and for the benefit of Their Honours, I would have to go back to the history of the inception of the military police force, in order for my answer to your questions to be properly understood. If you will allow me, I can briefly depict --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. And if it is necessary to make your answer understood, by all means, but I would certainly encourage you to make the background explanation as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. The specificity of both the Croatian army and the military police lay in the fact that it was the units that first came in existence and only then were the rules developed. The Croatian army was first constituted from members of the civilian police volunteers and then members of the National Guards Corps. It was only at that point that the Croatian army was formed also through the mobilisation of the reserve brigades. Each of these reserve brigades under its establishment had a military police battalion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Platoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And until such time as the military police was formed, and I have to tell you that I joined the forces in December 1991 by which time some hundred brigades of the Croatian army had been mobilised, these platoons were active in the area of the responsibility of that brigade, without any vertical subordination to any higher level military police structures. When I assumed my duties and gained insight into the military police structure, I found that there wasn't a single written rule governing the existence, work, or tasks of the military police force. The next step was to issue a provisional instructions governing the work of the military police which were in force until the 1994 rules were developed. The next stage was the stage of build up. These platoons, the military police platoons that were members of the reserve brigades remained part of these brigades under the establishment; but a vertical hierarchy was introduced, whereby they were subordinated to the MP companies and these, in turn, to MP battalions and then we also developed the territorial structure of the military police. We had operational zones, and I will use that term later on. These were transformed in Military Districts. And each of ease operational zones or areas had one MP battalion, and this battalion covered its area of responsibility through its respective companies and platoons and thus carried out their duties. This was the model which was in force until the disbandment of the reserve brigades. So my answer to your question is the platoons of the military police were members of the military police brigades under the establishment until such time as these brigades were disbanded. Vertically speaking, they were subordinate, in terms of -- they had their level of subordination, in terms of the professional line and everything else that this entails. They were subordinate to their -- to the companies. For this reason, the case that I illustrated earlier on could be resolved in such a way that the incident was reported on to the structures higher up in the system; and, of course, I tried to explain this in a few words, but I believe you can find this more extensively in both the interview and my witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lausic, thank you for that. I'm going also mention for guidance for future questions the Court now has your statement. It will be able -- that is part of your evidence. It's not necessary for the most part to repeat that unless you can certainly make reference to it in order to explain an answer, but we move faster if you bear in mind that the Court does have that information. And the -- I still may have misunderstood, but I don't I heard whether or not the situation that you just described, that is, with platoons attached to brigades, you said it was -- that was the model in force until the disbandment of the reserve brigades by 1995; and by the time of Operation Storm had those reserve brigades as you just described been disbanded, or did the situation that gave rise to the 1994 order, that is platoons within brigades, continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. If I could just -- this is light of what witness just answered, we're using terms like attached and disbanded. Attached may mean something specific and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can further explore that. At this moment I think the simple question is whether during -- at the time of Operation Storm, whether the reserve brigades has been disbanded already or not because that was part of the answer for which Mr. Tieger sought clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just as long it is understood what the witness's prior answer was with respect to what it means at that time to attach to a brigade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clearly on the record. But, Mr. Lausic, could you give an answer to the question put to you by Mr. Tieger, that whether in -- let's say August 1995, the reserve brigades during Operation Storm had been disbanded already or were still existing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reserve brigades were demobilised at a certain pace and then mobilised again, some in their entirety and some only in several elements. In August, when the preparations were under way for Operation Storm, I don't have the precise data here, but definitely the figure of more than 100.000 members of the Croatian army mobilised does indicates that a number of them were military policemen. I don't know when, but according to the new establishment of the reserve brigades, they no longer had military police platoons as part of their structure; though I don't have the precise figures here as to when the structure of the reserve brigades changed and when they no longer had as their part the military police platoons according to the so-called establishment book. These military police platoons were establishment-wise in the early days of the homeland war, in existence as soon as the reserve brigades were mobilised, and the establishment books of the reserve brigades had MP platoons as their part. Later on, as the structure of the reserve brigades changed, the establishment books no longer this MP platoons as part of their structure, so I can't tell you when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn back to Exhibit D35. Item 10 of D35. That is Minister of Defence Susak's order states that: "All orders regulating the system of command of military police units or manning of military police units in a manner contrary to the rules of the organisation work of the military police of the Main Staff of the -- of the Republic of Croatia, and to this order, shall cease to be in effect." I'd like to show you one -- one order and ask about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could we turn to D34, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And before we leave D -- sorry. I guess we just did. It's all right. Yeah, if we could just quickly -- I recited the terms of item 10 of D35 with the witness, but I'm not sure he had a chance to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, that's the item that I was referring to. I think it's on the screen now that: "All orders regulating the system of command of military police units in a manner contrary," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The witness seems to have a book of documents in front of him. If I could just inquire as to what he has in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. If I can answer that, Your Honour, then the witness can confirm or clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Prosecution did provide the witness with documents that it -- it might be using the during of the examination. I imagine that is what he has in front of him now. So not -- I don't think all of them are there, but at least some of those documents are now. The witness may have other documents with him that I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any documents in front of you not provided to you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I only have the documentation transcripts and witness statement, as well as the enclosed documentation I received from the Prosecutor before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine Mr. President. I just want to be clear that usually -- I have no problem with it. But I was just inquiring because usually the procedure is that the Registrar gives it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, usually it is that it is mentioned that hard copies were made available, but I have no view on the witness's table so -- hidden by two screens. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And thank you, Mr. Registrar. If we could turn to D34 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: D34 is on your screen at the moment, Mr. Lausic. It's entitled, "The Organisational Order Regarding Work, Order, and Discipline In Garrisons," was issued by Minister Susak, and General Bobetko, at that time, the chief of the Main Staff, And it's dated 27 August 1993; and, therefore, predates the order by Minister Susak we looked at a moment ago. If I could ask you -- I believe this is one of the documents provided before so you may have had a chance to look at that time, but it's an order that provides, among other things, as can you see at item 2, that: "The garrison commands do not have an operational function and the right to issue orders to Croatian army units, except precisely described authorities regarding work, order, and discipline in the garrison, outside of barracks and other military facilities, within the tasks provided by the rules of service of the armed forces." And it goes on to describe in item 3 that the garrison commands are required to establish cooperation and coordination, et cetera. First of all, Mr. Lausic, did you have a chance to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sometimes we have to wait for the translations to catch up. First of all, Mr. Lausic, did you have an opportunity to review this order in 1993 -- sorry. Did you have a chance to review this 1993 order before coming to court?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order - that is to say this document - is what I received on the 25th of January in the afternoon here at Scheveningen by Mr. Foster, alongside other documents I was handed over. Before that moment, I had never seen that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And my question is have you read it over or do I need to give you an opportunity to look at it in further detail right now?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent of the time I had on my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And my question, Mr. Lausic, is simply this: Is this order consistent or inconsistent with the rules of the organisation and work of the military police and the order by Minister Susak in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to say that Minister Susak's order dated the 6th of July, 1994 was the result of a specific event, which I described. It was issued in order to prevent such and similar incidents in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, excuse me, for a second and I just wanted in fairness to my colleagues I brought your attention to two particular items in D34; that is the 1993 order, but I should have also brought your attention to item 4 as well; and that is that the commanders of the Military Districts, the Croatian navy, the Croatian air force, and anti-aircraft defence shall study the enclosed directive in an organised fashion by 15 September 1993, and based on specific circumstances set out concrete tasks for each garrison regarding work order and discipline and the implementation of the prescribed tasks. In item 5 it continues that: "The commanders of the Military Districts and so on are required to monitor, work, order, and discipline in the garrisons through regular and interim inspections and checks and at least quarterly do an analysis of the situation of work, order, and discipline in the garrisons and based on the situation encountered take all necessary measures to bring work, order, and discipline in the garrison to the required level." Item 6 indicates the supervision of that implementation. There is an enclosure to that instruction, to that order as well, entitled, "Instructions on Regulating some Issues within the Jurisdiction of Garrisons." And if I could bring your attention to two of those. In the instructions at page 4 of the English, it's item number 4 in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would be at -- ERN page 0156-0259 of the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That item is entitled, "Employing Military Police Units," and states that: "The Military District --" excuse me, "The garrison commander is required to arrange a procedure with the closest unit of the military police of calling military police units and having them intervene in the case of unrest, accident, et cetera, when a MP unit is indispensable to establish order and discipline in the area of the garrison. Also, arrange for the temporary employment of military police patrols to supervise work, discipline, and conduct of military police in public places."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn next to item 17, found at page 7 of the English, and at the bottom of page 0156-0260 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's an item entitled, "Regulating Order, Discipline, and Supervision of the conduct of the military personnel," and begins: "The garrison commander shall lay down instructions on order, discipline, and supervision of the conduct of military personnel at the garrison that will cover," and then it has a list. Now having brought --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the list should be included as well in the question, if the witness is seeing this document for the -- maybe the second time since the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we give an opportunity to the witness to read the list. Mr. Lausic, would you please read that list as we find it in paragraph 17. You've read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So having brought further details of D34, the 27 August 1993 order, to your attention, let's me ask, Mr. Lausic, if there -- if that order is consistent or inconsistent with the -- or contrary or not contrary to the rules of the organisation and work of the military police and to Minister Susak's 1994 order.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I have to note the following: At the time this order was issued and signed by the minister of defence and chief of the General Staff, the rule on the work an organisation of the military police which we saw previously was not in force. It was put in force in February 1994. That is to say, four months later, or actually six months after this order. What was in use, however, was the document on the temporary rules on the organisation and work of the police that was put into force in January 1992 and was valid until the moment this -- these rules were put into place in February 1994; hence, they were termed temporary or interim instructions, although the period involved was that of two years. I mention that as both suspect and witness. It is also in the interview and my statement. Hence, there is no need for me to explain further. It was the first document defining the structure, powers, tasks and scope of authority of the military police, and now to go back to your question, in item 4 of the instructions on regulating some and certain issues that fall under the jurisdiction of garrisons attached to Minister Susak's and General Bobetko's order; in that item 4, where mention is made on the engagement of the units of the military police, the authority of command over the military police was given to the commander of the garrison involved. That person can be appointed personally or can be acting in such capacity according to the rules defined in the previous document. In Article 6 of the temporary instructions, we see what was later on regulated by the instructions which were brought into force later in Article 9. Unfortunately, much as many other others, this order was not implemented in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, as regards item 17, regulating order discipline and supervision of the conduct of military personnel, I'm not familiar with any garrison commander issuing a document to that effect. In order for you and the others present in the courtroom to understand these documents, I wanted to say that many of the rules of the Croatian army were actually copied from the JNA rules. Only certain terms were changed. Many of such orders and rules held no ground. It was realistically impossible to implement them, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The authority and obligations of the garrison commander with respect to the military police as outlined in the 1993 order and the attachments, was that the same or different than was provided under the 1994 rules?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything in item 4 that would be in dispute, as concerns the way a garrison commander organises and cooperates the -- with the units of the military police. I would have to go back to the rules on the work and operation of the military police dating from January 1992 that was in place until February 1994, in order to be able to answer your question precisely, whether Article 4 of these instructions, or this attachment includes all of the competences in the document you referred to. I believe that was Article 6. However, I do believe that it was the same, and I don't find anything odd about Article 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any confusion at this moment in relation to your question? Mr. Lausic, it seems that if you are comparing the 1993 order with the existing rules on the work an operation of the military police from January 1992, whereas, from what I understood, Mr. Tieger asked you but, please, correct me when I misunderstood you, Mr. Tieger, that Mr. Tieger wanted to know what you find in the 1993 order, whether that is in any way contrary to the rules that existed in 1994, being the rules of the organisation and work of the military police; that the question was, was there any reason -- that's again how I understood your question Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it would fall within the scope of item 10 of Minister Susak's order in 1994 that they should be -- that the order should cease to have effect because it was contrary with the rules of the organisation and work of the military police which were adopted in 1994. Is that what you wanted to know, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so a comparison with 1992 is not asked but whether these -- this 1993 order turned out to be in contradiction or contrary to the rules that were adopted in 1994. That's the first question. And the result perhaps being that under item 10, that, therefore, the order would cease to be in effect. You understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Presiding Judge, now I understand the question. The stipulations of Article 4 of the attachment and the order of Minister Susak and General Bobetko dating from August 1993 are not contrary to Article 9 of the rules of the work of the military police, dating back to February 1994. As regards the second part of your question, Minister Susak's order dated the 6th of July, 1994, does not have to do with the invalidation of this order. In item 10 of Mr. Susak's document, we see that all orders regulating the system of command or staffing of units that would be contrary to the rules of the organisation are deemed invalid. We also have to view this in the light of the fact why this command was issued. The minister, by virtue of his order, wanted to encompass any other possible similar commands that would go against the rules themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Lausic. I'd like to turn now to August of 1995 and D267 specifically. Mr. Lausic, I believe you'll recognise D267. This is an order issued on the 2nd of August, 1995, by you to -- to various military police battalions and also delivered, as we see, after your signature to many persons, including Minister Susak, General Cervenko, the commanders of various Military Districts, and so on. The subject of the order is preparations of military police units to perform military police tasks in areas of responsibility of the Croatian army, Military Districts during the upcoming operations. And then the order follows. If could I bring your attention first the first two items in the order, items 3 and 4. Item 3 appears to be directed to the setting up of forward command posts of military police battalion with all necessary officers and equipment, and it provides in the last sentence: "Within the daily operational chain of command, commanders of military police battalions shall be subordinated to commanders of the Croatian army Military Districts." Item 4 addresses itself to the setting up of forward command posts of military police companies in the -- that are in the areas of responsibility of operative groups. And similarly indicates: "Within the daily operational chain of command, company commanders shall be subordinated to commanders of the Croatian army Operational Groups?" Now, again, Mr. Lausic, the reference to the subordination to the commanders, is that a reference to Article 9 or any other Article within the rules.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no direct reference to the rules. An order is being issued. It is very precise. It is the so-called preparatory command or order to all MP units to carry out their tasks in the areas of responsibility of various Croatian army units of in the forthcoming operations. It has to do with my previous order on raising of the state of readiness of all MP units. It is true that in item 3 of this order I order that MP battalion commanders should establish forward command posts at forward command posts of the Military Districts, which is only logical. If we are referring to the 72nd Battalion, the forward command post of the Split Military District was in Sajkovici, and by virtue of this order, I ordered that the commander of the 72nd Battalion establish his forward command post at the same location rather than staying in Split. This was in order to link up the two respective commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like him to finish that answer, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tieger is entitled to bring the witness back to the question he has put --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to him, and if there is it any further matter. Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If at the very end of your testimony you think you have had -- not had an opportunity to explain a matter you find important, of course, you'll have an opportunity to add anything. I take it that Mr. Tieger wants to take you back to the question because his question was primarily focussing on whether the -- what we find in this order, whether this is it -- whether this order in this respect is given in the legal context of Article 9 of the rules, or whether there was any other legal context or legal basis for issuing this order, and we are focussing on paragraphs 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I understand now. Absolutely all of the items of this order are in keeping with the rules on -- on the structure and work of the military police, and item 8 of that document delegating scope of authority of the head of the military police; and Article 9, which deals with regular military police tasks and handing over command over those units to respective Military District Commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now perhaps, is there in any particular portion of 3 and 4, is there some, what you say they -- are directly related to Article 8 or Article 9; are they all under Article 8; are they all under Article 9. If you'd like it make a distinction between the different portions of paragraph 3 and 4, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I issued this order pursuant to my authority, based on Article 8 of the rules on the structure and work of the military police. In Articles 3 and 4, I used the authority stipulated in Article 9 handing over command to the various commanders of military districts and operational groups. There is nothing in dispute here. This order is based on the rules of the structure and work of the military police containing all of the competencies I held as head of the military police based on Article 8. And I delegated the rights mentioned therein to the specified commanders in order for them to be able to command over the units which had been resubordinated to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I guess my question would be this, Article 9 seems to indicate that while performing regular military police tasks, those units of are subordinate to the commander of the Military District by virtue of the rules. Why was it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's a very technical thing, but it is not quite accurate to say they're subordinate to. And this is something that will come up in cross, and it is actually in the witness's statement, and I don't want to give testimony in front of the witness; but if it could just be read exactly as it appears in Article 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- unless there's a translation discrepancy I will read it again. But I thought it was read accurately at that time. Article 9 states: "While performing their regular military police task, military police units are subordinate to the commander of the Military District, the commander of the Croatian navy, the commander of the Croatian air force, or to the highest Croatian army commander by function in the military police units' area of operations."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So my question is this, Mr. Lausic: If you hadn't issued the order stating that within the daily operational chain of command commanders of the military police battalions shall be subordinated to commanders of the Croatian army Military Districts, would Article 9, nevertheless, have made those units subordinate to the commanders of the Military Districts. In other words, were you doing anything more in this order than was provided for in Article 9?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, the order only uses a different term by saying within the daily operational chain of command rather than saying while performing their regular military police tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could turn your attention next to item 10 of the order. That's found on page 4 of the English, and I imagine won't be difficult to find in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It starts at the bottom of page 2. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Item 10, Mr. Lausic, is the appointment of Major Cvitanovic, Major Juric and Colonel Kozic. And specifically with respect to Major Juric found at the second paragraph : "I appoint Major Ivan Juric and a group of officers from the regular military police section and the military police administration crime section to assist in commanding and organising the activities of the 72nd Military Police Battalion and 73rd Split Military Police Battalion that shall perform tasks in its own area of responsibility and provide necessary assistance to the 72nd Military Police Battalion. The commanders of the 72nd Military Police Battalion and 73rd Military Police Battalion shall be subordinated to Major Ivan Juric." Now your statement addresses the appointment of Major Juric at paragraphs 162 through 164 and that, indeed, you specifically discussed this order in paragraphs 162 through 167; but I simply wanted to ask you whether the appointment of Major Juric was an interference with or limitation of the authority of the Military District Commanders under Article 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object as to vagueness. I don't know what that specific means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, was there anything inconsistent then -- I don't mind -- I would wait for a ruling, Your Honour, but I don't mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you rephrase the question, if that would meet the concern, that sometimes takes less time and avoids a risk that someone else might consider the question to be vague as well. Therefore, if you could meet without a ruling, I would prefer that. Otherwise I give the ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is there anything inconsistent with your appointment of Major Juric for the purposes specified in your order with the powers conferred on the Military District Commanders under Article 9? In other words, were you intruding on their powers; were you exceeding your own authority?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to first give an introduction and an explanation as to why I decided to set up forward command posts of the military police. As early as during Operation Flash, I noticed that there was a discrepancy between the orders issued, according to the methodology and tactics of the conduct of the military police, and the situation on the ground. I gleaned that from my stay on the ground. Since a great number of soldiers was to be engaged for the purposes of Operation Storm, I decided to have my own ears and eyes on the ground, so to speak, in order to have my own officers at forward command posts, officers from the MP administration. And I did as much as was mentioned in the order. I set up three forward command posts and manned them with officers from the MP administration. Their quality as officers can be gleaned from their professional career, which continues to this day. There is nothing inconsistent or contrary in the powers. I conferred upon these officers, stationed at IKMs of the military police administration, or in the powers conferred upon Major Juric as the person number one of the forward command post of the MP administration. In this way, I conferred some of my powers granted to me under Article 8 to him as one of the officers from the MP administration. The tasks he was given, the reporting system, or all of that is contained in my 2nd of August order, which can also be found in the documentation belonging to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask but that reporting system which I believe is indicated at item 12, found beginning at the bottom of page 4 of the English and page 3 of the Croatian. All right. It's broken down into three paragraphs, the first one indicates that: "Within the daily operational chain of command, commanders of military police battalions, commanders of the 69th, the 70th, and 74th Military Police Companies shall be subordinated to commanders of the Croatian army Military Districts, commanders of the navy and air force; and they shall report to them in writing and at briefings on a daily basis." And the second paragraph goes on to indicate that every day at 2000 hours and it lists various commanders of battalions and companies who shall report to the military police administration until 2000 hours every day, starting from 4 August 1995. So was that setting up a parallel or two-part reporting system?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going object, Your Honour, as to leading. There is a non-leading way to put that, and that is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, can you just explain the purpose of the two paragraphs and the two -- and the kinds of reporting that you set in place under item 12.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 12 of the order sets forth in more -- with more precision the command and reporting systems, in order to remove any vagueness that may have arisen out of the setting up of the forward command posts of the MP administration. As paragraph 1 of item 12 states, commanders of the military police battalion, commanders of the 69th, the 70th, and 74th Companies of the military police, and these were companies with the Bjelovac and Karlovac Military Districts and the Croatian air force, shall be subordinated within the daily operational chain of command to the commanders of the Military Districts, the commander of the HRM and HRZ and shall report to them every day in writing and at briefings. Then the commanders of the 66th which was in Zagreb, then the seat of the military police and the 74th Company of the military police shall report to the chief of the MP administration directly everyday by 2000 hours with the situation as of 1900 hours. And then the commanders of the 67th and the 69th Company, Major Cvitanovic was from the Sisak Military District of the MP administration; then the commanders of the 70th Company, that was one from Karlovac; and the 71st MP Battalion, which was the Gospic Military District, Colonel Damir Kozic; and he was the leader of the IKM of the MP in Ogulin; and the commanders of the 72nd Battalion and the 73rd Battalion of the military police, the 73rd being with the navy, the Major Ivan Juric; and he was the person number one at the IKM of the MP administration in Sajkovici; whereas Damir Kozic, and Major Juric, and Major Cvitanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If could you direct your attention to the basic structures rather than the details which are contained within the order itself and just describe the basic reporting system that you were setting up through this order rather than the specific persons to whom it was directed or the -- the specific companies or battalions involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, as I understand what Mr. Tieger would like to know is the following: Whether, in this document, we find that reporting was ordered, both in the HV hierarchy, these Military Districts, and also in the hierarchy of the military police administration, so the two going at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is that any different than the reporting system that was in place under normal circumstances, prior to Storm and after Storm?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object to the complete lack of precision in how questions are being posed. That question is so broad and has so means different elements to it. Reporting system in what line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have to be talking specific -- let me just [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Precision is lacking Mr. Misetic; then there is ample opportunity to make it more precise and if that would invalidate the answer; and, of course, that should be clear on the record, if you, Mr. Lausic, at any moment consider a question to be so imprecise that you couldn't answer it, ask for the type of precision you would need to be able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I can just make my objection for the record then, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The order say what it says. It does not say reporting. If we're going to use the proper terminology, I would request, it says daily operational chain versus something else. There are more documents here, and I'm trying to make sure that there is no ambiguity that's being created in how the questions are being phrased. I understand if we are going to go through all this in cross-examination, Your Honour, that's fine. But my objection is still just to note for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What Mr. Tieger, as far as I understand, but forgive me, Mr. Tieger for now and then trying to repeat your questions so as to verify there is no misunderstanding of the question; what Mr. Tieger apparently would like to know is whether this system, in which reports were ordered to be sent within the HV Military District hierarchy and the military police hierarchy, whether this simultaneous reports to be sent in these two hierarchical lines, whether that existed also before Operation Storm -- may I take it, Mr. Tieger, you wanted to refer prior to the 2nd of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Prior to 2nd of August and after Operation Storm. And if you have any difficulty in understanding when Operation Storm was over, tell us whether it continued to exist and up till what moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. All the battalions of the military police, as well as the independent companies of the military police, were supposed to send a regular daily report to the duty service of the MP administration by 2400 hours for everyday; and it was on the basis of that report that the duty service department compiled a morning bulletin about all the events in all the AORs of the Croatian army; and that was provided to the highest levels of the state, not only the Ministry of Defence but also specifically the -- office of the president. This order, in addition to the regular reporting system, daily reporting system which remains in force, and that's to say the duty services of the battalions and companies which continued to submit regular daily reports, this order puts into place a commanding and reporting system on a daily basis at briefings with commanders of the Military Districts, as well as other functions mentioned herein. Whereas the reporting to -- toward the MP administration by the battalions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment because everything you said until now was well understood from your previous answers and from the content of this order. What Mr. Tieger wants to know is were you ordered, this additional, as you called it, commanding and reporting system for the -- for the commanders of the Military Districts; you ordered that that would be put in place additionally 2nd of August, until when did that additional command and reporting system exist? Did it continue to exist after Operation Storm, and tell us when, in your view, Operation Storm has ended; or was it at any moment in time, was it discontinued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't be precise, but there is my -- my order exists in the documentation about the dissolving of the forward command posts and the reintroduction of the regular reporting system. However, this system contained in item 12 was in force until such time as the forward command posts were, whether it was on the 16th of August or thereabouts, dissolved; and the regular reporting system was the only system that remained in place as it had been in existence previously, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that an answer to your question, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I -- yes and no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If have you any further questions, of course, I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And under that regular reporting system, Mr. Lausic, do you know whether Military District Commanders received briefings and reports from the commanders of military police battalions; and, if so, with what frequency?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the first tasks that the MP administration carried out immediately upon the inception, and I will have to go back to the years when the MP administration came into existence, was that we set up a reporting system toward the military police administration from the military police units. The first organisational form thereof that was set up in the administration was the operational duty section. This was, I believe, in February 1992, unless I'm mistaken, which was active around the clock and received reports. The system became perfected as the military police itself developed and improved in quality. It had daily reports according to all the various segments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are going in a lot of details in the answers where the question is apparently not aiming at receiving these details. May I invite you to first give an answer to the question, without the details, and if there's any need for the details, or if at the very end of your testimony you say, This detail should be known to the Court, an opportunity will be given to you. But what Mr. Tieger, and I do the same exercise again, apparently wants to know is that in the ordinary situation where report is in the hierarchy of the military police administration; and where we did not have the additional order as we find it in the 2nd of August order to command and report system, as you said within the Military Districts, in this ordinary system, would there be any information that went up the line, would that, and if so, at what interval would that be reported to in the military structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to say that. Every report that was sent toward or to the duty service of the MP administration was, at the same time, sent to the commander who was -- who had jurisdiction territorially speaking whether it was the commander of the -- of a Military District, the commander of the navy, or the commander of the unit that was active in the AOR. So while the report was sent to the duty service of the MP administration, it would also be sent to the commander of a given unit or an organisational unit of the Croatian army. It would also be sent to a third body, the competent state administration -- state competent police administration because I would be sending a bulletin that we produced to the Ministry of Interior, and they, in turn, would be sending their reports to us. The commander of the Military District would be sending a report to the chief of the police administration. We were in charge of a given area as civilian and military police structures respectively and had to exchange information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And just to make sure that I understood your answer well, what you now described existed also prior to the 2nd of August and also after the forward command posts were not in existence anymore. You gave as an indication 16th of August. Is that how I have to understand your answer in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The system was in place throughout the Operation Storm, including the period starting from the 2nd of August when the order was issued, up until the dissolution of the forward command posts. This was the constant system of reporting that was not discontinued at any time, and it was for the purposes of this operation. Another such system was introduced for Operation Maslenica, Flash as it was for Storm; and all these respective orders introduced an extraordinary reporting system since the situation requiring it was an extraordinary one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, I did not -- you may not have understood the question accurately and therefore, perhaps, I may have misunderstood your question. Mr. Tieger, perhaps a matter to be clarified after the break because we will first have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one thing I would like to put on the record with the witness not being present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, we will have a break, and we will resume in 25 minutes from now. Mr. Misetic would like to address the Court, and I invite you already to follow the usher and leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me state to the extent that I misunderstood the witness's testimony then I apologise in advance. However there has been much evidence and many reports to the military police both submitted into evidence here and disclosed to us by the Office of the Prosecutor. I don't know of any documents that would substantiate what this witness has just testified about in terms of the reporting. Putting it as politically correct as I can, the reason I was objecting to the broad questions is that the witness should not be invited to state matters that the parties know or should have reason to know has no evidentiary support, and to that extent those documents are in evidence. If there is something to be put to him on paper about such reports of operational matters going both to Mr. Lausic and either to Mr. Gotovina or Mr. Cermak, then it should be put to him. But to do this in a manner that floats broad questions that allows this witness to make all sorts of assertions that are contrary to what the parties already have in the case, I believe, is improper, and I will state it that way; and if I miss stood what Mr. Lausic has said then I apologise both tho him and to counsel. But that is my understanding of the testimony we have just heard. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question directed itself to a particular document and ordered by the witness in asking to explicate that document. What was meant and intended by this particular order and then ask him to explain the extent to which, if any, the order that he was describing differed from the system that had preceded it or followed it. Now the question of the extent to which that may or may not have been implemented, the extent to which documents exist which confirm how well it was pursued seems to be an entirely separate matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is it entirely on the document from which we are to gather what the state of the evidence is in the case. The reason that I was asking for precision is that the order says in the daily operational matters which as the Chamber will know has been significantly disputed not least of which the testimony of Mr. Theunens that is going to be gone into in more detail with Mr. Lausic in cross-examination. However, it's why I insisted to say that commanders of zones are being briefed on daily operational matters. There's also a document in evidence about what reporting Mr. Lausic wanted to get from Mr. Juric, and the proper way to put this to him would have been to show him that document and then say either, Did you order that this information also go to the zone commanders, and if not why not? But to allow witness to make all sorts of claims when we all know the state of the evidence in the case, again I will be discrete an say is an improper way to put matters to a witness and can lead to a situation where false information is being put before the Chamber. And that is my objection. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do see that the state of the evidence is not an easy concept to use under the present circumstances, and I take it that if Mr. Tieger sees the state of the evidence in its totality would invalidate most of the answers, then he would be prudent enough, I would say, not to take such risks; whereas, of course, there are other elements in the evidence which Mr. Tieger apparently wants to further explore, which is his good right to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. President, and that's why I laid a preparatory apology in advance. However there is also just the factual matter in terms of the discovery between the parties. If I'm wrong and there are, in fact, reports, written reports for the witness said on a daily basis going -- the same reports as I understand it going both to the military police administration and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was just asking to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm warned that if we do not take a break now that we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A revolt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A justified revolt. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the better expression. We'll have a break, and we resume at 4.30. And with the apologies to everyone who was suffering from my lack of decisiveness on taking the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to briefly come back to something I said on page 14718, in relation to B/C/S translations of documents that were tendered by the Defence in English. I expressed some concern, not for the B/C/S version not to be available to the accused because I take it that that right is waived, if the Defence introduces such a document in English only, but about the public character of the trial. And I said that we'll consider whether we'll ask for a translation to be provided. Now, having further considered the matter, the Chamber is satisfied that usually the content of a document becomes sufficiently clear during the examination of a witness; and that, therefore, for the purpose of the public character of the trial, that it's not necessary to insist on a translation. And if it might still remain not very clear because if it's a very short answer then, of course, the parties are invited to consider to add one or two lines just to explain what we are doing because the Chamber is focussing very much on the public character of the trial; but sometimes the remedy would be disproportionate to the problem; and, therefore, as a rule, the Chamber will not insist on translations, and the Chamber is also aware of the problems in having them prepared, efforts involved. That's one. The second issue I would like to briefly raise is that the parties are urged - at this moment Defence, perhaps in the near future Prosecution - to limit the objections to what is necessary and to not unnecessarily disrupt the flow of evidence, if the matter can be dealt with in cross-examination as well. This being on the record, Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Tieger, once the witness has taken the stand again, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, Mr. Tieger will now continue his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, before we move on, I want to make as short as possible that we all understand the evidence you were providing just before the break. So I'm going to ask some short and hopefully simple questions that can be answered very briefly to make sure that we're as clear as we can be. You looked at the -- at your August 2nd order and specifically item 12, and you described the reporting system that you ordered at that time. So that reporting system provided for reports both to you at the military police administration, and to the Military District Commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before the order was issued, and after the order was no longer operative, because Storm was over, did reports go from the military police both to you, at the military police administration, and to the Military District Commanders?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I would also like to add that the same situation applied during the course of this period -- this order's period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When -- in your order, when you say in item 12 that: "The commanders of military police battalion, commanders of the 69th Military Police Company, the 70th, the 74th Company shall be subordinated to the commanders of the Military Districts, and they shall report to them in writing and at briefings on a daily basis," what sort of information were you -- what sort of information were the commanders of military police battalions and the commanders of the companies supposed to provide to the Military District Commanders?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All reports on executed tasks, pursuant to orders that may have been issued by those Military District Commanders as well as on other tasks implemented by the MP units in the course of their regular activities within a given area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were the Military District -- military police battalion commanders and the company commanders supposed to provide the Military District Commanders with information about their execution of military police tasks, pursuant to Article 10?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. They had to report on all of their activities. That is to say, within each reporting period. They had to report on everything they had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What information did you get back during the course of -- let me ask it this way. From the time you issued this order, that is D267 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, perhaps it's better to understand if you say the 2nd of August order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because that is what the witness understands. So from the time you issued the 2nd of August order. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What information did you receive, Mr. Lausic, about the extent to which the reporting that you had ordered was being fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without being able to refer to specific reports that are in the documents -- among the documents in my binder, I cannot tell you anything precisely. I would have to refer to those first. In any case, as regards the reporting, they were supposed to report on all of the activities their respective units within a given territory as well as on certain other specific issues such as insufficient staffing, lack of equipment, problems they may have encountered into the implementation of tasks, as well as some other specific situations, which may have changed from one report to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you receive any complaints from any Military District Commanders that the military police were not reporting to them on a daily basis about what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive such information or reports. Well, those would not be reports, per se, because the Military District Commanders would turn to their superiors and I would only have to be notified. I'm trying to use specific terms and terminology. They were duty-bound to report to their superiors. To put it briefly, I did not receive such information from Military District Commanders or other operational structures of the armed forces on the problem of reporting by MP unit commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn next to -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lausic, I also wanted to turn my attention to one part of the transcript, and that was at 34:15 of today's transcript, in the course of an answer that -- transcript says -- you said according to the transcript: "The commander of the Military District would be sending a report to the chief of the police administration. We were in charge of a given area as civilian and military police structures respectively and had to exchange information." Was that correct, that it's the commander of the Military District who would be sending a report to the chief of the police administration?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question, and I don't seem to recall that part of the transcript. I'm not certain about the answer I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me just -- setting aside the question of the transcript, let me ask that you question about reporting responsibilities. First of all, was -- were reports about what the military police was doing shared with the chiefs of police administrations; and, if so, whose responsibility was it to provide that information to the chiefs of police administrations?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to clarify -- let me ask -- ask it one more time in a slightly different way. Was the commander of the Military District, insofar as you were aware, required to send a report to either you, as the chief of the military police administration, or to the chief of the civilian police administration?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Military District Commander was in no case duty-bound to send such reports to me as the head of administration or to the chiefs of administration of the civilian police. Perhaps I was misunderstood. I was referring to the commanders of battalions who sent their daily reports as part of the regular reporting system to the competent chief of the civilian police administration. It was the same as received by the police administration at headquarters. The exchange of information between the military police and the civilian police went on at the highest level; that is to say, at the level of ministries. We established the same system within the respective areas, the responsibility of military police battalions, companies, and their counterparts in the civilian police. However, I did not intend to include Military District Commanders. I was referring to the commanders of the MP battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn next to something that was discussed briefly yesterday, and something that is addressed in your statement at paragraphs 146 through 151 of your statement. There's a discussion of the meeting on August 2nd which took place at 10.00 in the Republic of Croatia Defence Ministry war room, and I believe you clarified one aspect of that with the Court yesterday. That's D409, is the entry, the diary entry from your diary, which reflects notes from that meeting, which state: "Military police must be more energetic in its actions and must prevent all offences. Military District Commanders must be the ones to pass on to the other commanders the prohibition of any kind of uncontrolled conduct (torching, looting, et cetera) --" this is quoting -- these are notes taken in reference to Minister Susak. And then the comment you clarified with the Court yesterday, we must prevent from taking the heros of the homeland war to court. Now I would like to turn your attention quickly to D45.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could call that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a record of a working meeting held in the grand conference room of the Ministry of Defence on the 3rd of August, 1995. And at page 5 of the English and page 2 of the Croatian, the record of the meeting reflects remarks by you in your introductory address. And it indicates that you spoke about the meeting of the ministers which had been held the previous day which included the meeting -- included the highest officials an officers of the Croatian army, and it noted that it had, among others, rendered the military police and the MUP responsible for complete efficiency in carrying out tasks: "During combat activities of the Croatian army, he" -- that's you, according to this note, "he also pointed out that the commanders of the HV units were warned that they would personally be responsible for the discipline of their subordinates otherwise not even a much larger number of the military police force would be able to secure discipline." I wanted to ask you, Mr. Lausic, if this is an accurate reflection of what you said to the group on August 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did it accurately convey what was said at the previous day's meeting of the ministers and highest officials and officers of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. In my notes from the meeting in the war room of the Defence Ministry dated the 2nd of August, which, in turn, was copied from my personal diary, what we have are the exact words of Minister Susak. If I may, I just want to find that note of mine for the sake of precision when quoting his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you're having any difficulty finding that, Mr. Lausic, we can call it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask that you do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we call up D409, please.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it. Could we please enlarge it so that I could read? That is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it should be the -- the entry on page 3 of the English, and I believe the same in the Croatian, but we'll need to check.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found my notes. Perhaps I can refer to the written material I have before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it looks like that was roughly simultaneous. It's also up on the screen, Mr. Lausic, if you -- so either way.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under Minister Gojko Susak, meaning that I took down his words, as he was addressing us, we find the following: "In the Republic of Croatia 52.000 men were mobilised (total: 170.000)." It says that: "A meeting was held with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council and the movement is in the direction of Donji Vakuf and Kulen Vakuf. The HVO is moving toward Banja Luka (action commending on 3 August 1995). "Military police must be more energetic in its actions and must prevent all offences. Military District Commanders must be the ones to pass on to the other commanders the prohibition of any kind of uncontrolled conduct (torching, looting, et cetera). We must prevent having to take the heros of the homeland war to court. Workers of the ideological and political department must carry out their tasks of appropriately briefing HV members. "The west has given a partial blessing but nothing must happen to UNPROFOR." Those were the main points from Minister Susak's intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, the next day at the working meeting, you said as I understand it from the record of that meeting and from your answer a few moments ago, that the commanders of the HV units were warned that they would personally be responsible for the discipline of their subordinates. Is that something that Minister Susak or someone else said, or is that something that you understood Minister Susak or someone else to have said, based on the comments reflected in your notes?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting with my colleagues from the Ministry of Interior, when the basic concept of cooperation was agreed for the forthcoming operation, what I did was brief them in shortest possible terms on the meeting of the previous day. I did focus on several items, including this one; and that is to say, that the commanders of HV units were told that they would be personally responsible for the conduct of their subordinates, because without that, even with a far greater number of military policemen, discipline could not be ensured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn next to D506, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: D506 is a document dated the 9th of August, 1995, which was sent by you, Mr. Lausic, to Minister Susak; General Cervenko; director of HIS, Dr. Tudjman; Brigadier Rebic, chief of political administration; Tolj; and chief of SIS, Gugic regarding the use of military police during Operation Storm. And if I could -- this is a document that I believe you referred to at paragraph 201 of your statement, and I wanted to direct your attention to the second page in English and also the second page in Croatian, where you state: "There are grave problems because of the large number of HV members in the settlements, and their commanders do not excerpt influence over them so that there are attempts at random plunder and burning of buildings. "We propose that appropriate measures be taken along the line of command so that the line of command would prevent plunder, the burning of buildings and similar acts that harm the reputation of the HV." Can you explain to the Court, Mr. Lausic, what you meant when you reported to Minister Susak, General Cervenko, and the others that: "There are grave problems, and the commanders do not excerpt influence over the HV members in the settlements."

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, one needs to say that these reports were being sent to the addressees mentioned as of day one of Operation Storm, although this was not expressly requested from me. However, when one reports to one's superiors, one also transfers the responsibility to them. By doing so, I wanted to point out the portion of tasks of the military police albeit it limited in terms of staff and equipment as well as the problems we were encountering making our tasks more difficult. I also wanted to point out that there is a need to see measures be put in place along the lines of command which would prevent the commission of crimes and unsoldierly behaviour. In each of my reports and the last paragraph; and this includes this particular report; and that would be item 6, I put in suggestions and requests. I mentioned that I suggested and requested that the line of command be used to ensure supervision over HV members in the liberated territory. By this, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, please continue. By that ...

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to notify the highest military officials, that is to say, the chief of General Staff. I wanted to point out the importance of doing that in order that measures be undertaken that fall within his remit in order to increase the level, the rules of service are being implemented in the field as well as to include all of the aspects that pertain to the life and work of the armed forces. If I may continue. You can also find that in my witness statement. It was at that time that I believed, as I do know, that the military police, even had we had far more men in the field, and even with much more equipment and education of our staff, could not have been efficient if the line of command was dysfunctional. And we had daily examples of that, of conduct that went against the rules of service as well as other regulations pertains to life and work of the armed forces. Many such examples are mentioned in our activities, reports, and we have numbers that refer to actions being taken by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you use the term "line of command," is that the line of command of the HV, of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The line or chain of command starting from the squad leader, platoon leader, company commander, all the way up to the Military District Commander. The more dysfunctional the chain of command is, the lesser the possibility that the military police will be able to resolve the problem, regardless of the level of its equipment, training; particularly keeping in mind the fact that across the 7.000 square kilometres of the newly liberated territory, I had some 1200 military policemen and all of them were engaged on the 12th/12th basis which means they were on duty for 12 hours, and then 12 hours, they had rest which were basically taken up by them going to work or going off duty and taking time to eat. When I analyse the numbers of the military policemen that I had to cover the newly liberated area, the equipment they had, the level of training that they had undertaken, all of that is found in the documentation that I handed over to the OTP in May 2004. And I believe that these analyses that I produced can be found in the case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you say in your report of August 9th that you propose -- it says, "We propose that appropriate measures be taken along the line of command," did you have particular measures in mind that should be taken by the line of command to bring the HV members in line.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every HV commander at all levels of command had at their disposal all the legal instruments that were valid at the time in Croatia, governing the armed forces in Croatia. These provisions could be found in the collection of legal regulations governing all aspects of life of the Croatian army from the use of combat vehicles to the organisation of the internal service, signing up for equipment, handing equipment over, to all the other details I don't wish to go into now. But all these details had to be taken into consideration by a commander, and this was not compiled with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 201 of your statement, I believe it indicates that this report was based upon "reports that we would receive from the ground."
