And -- but in paragraph 239, it -- your statement indicates that when you spoke with Major Juric on August 8th, he didn't mention anything about problems, and his reports, at least the ones that you had with you at the time that you were making the statement, were not particularly alarming. So I wanted to ask you what information you received in the reports that you referred to in paragraph 201; that is, the reports from the ground, that prompted the report of August 9th?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to note that the reports I sent these bodies quite high up, the Ministry of Defence, the Main Staff, and other relevant bodies of the Republic of Croatia, were not solely based on the reports from Major Juric, who was the head of the forward command post of the MP with the Split Military District HQ; but also on the reports from the other two commanders of the MP forward command post, Cvitanovic and Kozic, as well as other commanders of the military police, including the reports that I received orally or in writing from members of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, if I may, to another document issued around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P203.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, P203 is an information report from Colonel Gugic to Minister Susak and to Dr. Tudjman. And if I can direct your attention to the third paragraph which refers to events in various places, including, Kistanje. It states: "Incidents of mass burning of houses, plundering of property, alcohol consumption occur, and the units lack organisation. The reason for such a situation is the insufficient engagement of the command personnel of the units." Now, first, Mr. Lausic, I wanted to ask you if you were aware of this report at or shortly after the time it was sent?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of it. I saw this document for the first time on the 25th, in the afternoon hours, when I received it as part of the documentation brought to me by Mr. Foster.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you otherwise informed about the events referred to in the document?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Minister Susak or Colonel Gugic ever tell you that there were incidents of mass burning of houses and plundering of property at or about that time?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, save for this one encounter that I was an eye-witness of quite by chance on the staircase of the Ministry of Defence where there was General Cervenko, chief of the Main Staff, and Minister Susak. I happened to be there by chance. Minister Susak warned General Cervenko in an angry voice, Introduce some order into that army of yours. What's that army doing? I don't remember when exactly this happened. I know it was during -- at the time of Operation Storm. I think that this, too, can be found in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it's --

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps in a different rhetoric feature of speech, but it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's at paragraph 213. Did you ask Minister Susak what information he had that prompted this comment and whether or not you were in possession of the information about the location of the events that had triggered his anger and the units involved?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment in time, I thought that Minister Susak reacted in this way toward General Cervenko primarily in view of the reports that I was sending him. But it would have been improper of me to ask the minister of defence to explain his outburst.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me return for a moment to D506. That's the report of August 9th, Mr. Lausic. You indicated earlier that you made certain recommendations and requests and directed the Court's attention to those. Those are found at point 6 of your report, at the end of the document, which would be page 4 of the Croatian and also page 4 of the English. And as you noted that -- those recommendations and requests include not only providing supervision of members of HV units through the chain of command, but also the first listed recommendation or request which states: "In order to carry out military police assignments in the liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia, especially for searches (sweeps) of the liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia of enemy remnants, please withdraw all military police units from combat activities and engage them on carrying out military police assignments." Now, was that recommendation, Mr. Lausic, related to the information you had that there were grave problems because of burning of buildings and random plunder and commanders were not exerting influence over HV members?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry I apologise. I don't follow the -- it's a leading question, and I don't follow the connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the first part of the report, Your Honour, Mr. Lausic, noted these problems. And then he makes a recommendation to withdraw the military police units from combat activities and engage them in carrying out military police assignments, and I wanted to know if that recommendation was related to that part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, that's not how I read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is a matter of reading, let's do it literally so as to avoid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I will try again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, again I want to bring your attention to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the first portion had been read.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We find that in order to carry out, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then earlier in your report you had stated: "There are grave problems because of the large number of HV members in the settlements and their commanders do not excerpt influence offer them so that there are attempts at random plunder and burning of buildings."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, again I apologise but I think Mr. Tieger is misreading the paragraph, and if just ask the witness first what he meant by that. And if the connection is what Mr. Tieger suggests --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could at least ask witness to take headphones off, and I will explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although he understands English, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll try to be cryptic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Be as cryptic as you ca, Mr. Misetic. Could you take your earphones -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think what it suggests is the first portion, the first part of the sentence about I think it is saying to withdraw them so that the sweeps can take place, not withdraw them, which are currently engaged in sweeps. So to the extent that Mr. Tieger is saying did you withdraw in order to do something else other than what the paragraph explicitly says the purpose of withdrawing them is for --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand Mr. Misetic's point. I don't agree, but I have no problem asking completely non-leading questions. I don't think that was unfairly leading. I think it was appropriately linked but to eliminate any possible problem, I will ask the question in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, turning your attention to the first recommendation in item 6, what did you have in mind of making that recommendation? What was the purpose of asking to have the military police units withdrawn from combat activities and engage in carrying out military police assignments?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly, in order to reinforce the military police forces charged with carrying out these military policing tasks. Combat tasks were priorities of a lower level, so to speak, of the military police. The military police was engaged in combat, and this was outlined in detail in the document compiled on the 15th of August and addressed to General Cervenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the recommendation says that you -- that it was in order to carry out military police assignments in the liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia, especially for searches or sweeps; so I think we understand that there was an interest in having the military police engage in searches or sweeps. Let me also ask you if the recommendation to withdraw the military police units from combat activities was also related in any way to the information you had that there were grave problems because of the attempts at random plunder and burning of buildings?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This request, which was sent to the chief of the Main Staff, was based on the information received from the field about the increasing lack of discipline, the increasing numbers of incidents of plundering, and stealing property, et cetera, et cetera. But also on the basis of the fact that the military police could now move on from the two-shift method of work to the three-shift method of work, which meant that they would not work on the basis of the 12/12 hours but 12/24 hours. So, firstly, to reinforce the forces to carry out the tasks that were impending but also to enable them to have longer periods of rest by introducing the three-shift method of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to D837, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, D837 is an order by you on 9th of August. Subject is disengagement of the military police units from combat activities, and the first item in the order is: "All military police units engaged in combat activities are to be disengaged from the areas of combat activities at 0700 hours on 10 August 1995." It's submitted to Minister Susak, to General Cervenko, to Brigadier Rebic, and to the commanders of all the Croatian army Military Districts. If could you clarify for the Court, on the 9th of August we have your report to Minister Susak and others recommending that the military police be withdrawn from combat. On the same date, we have this order ordering that military police units be disengaged, sent to the minister of defence, and the commanders of the Military Districts, and also to the battalions as we see listed on the first page of the order. Can you explain to the Court exactly how that worked, that there was a recommendation and an order in the same day?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports we commented upon earlier on, including the 9 August report, were sent normally at 7.00 in the morning. In relation to this recommendation that military police units be disengaged from combat and engaged in military policing activities, I very soon received consent from the minister of defence and the chief of the Main Staff and issued an order to commence the disengagement of military police units from combat. For these reasons, the -- both the report and the order carry the same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could look quickly at 1208, P1208. And that's an order dated the 10th of August, the next day, from General Gotovina, on the basis of your order from the previous day, ordering that all the units of military police and anti-terrorist platoons engaged in the combat activities are to be withdrawn immediately from the zone of combat operations and returned to the original military police units. And that: "Military police and anti-terrorist units will be engaged according to a special plan in the search and sweep operation in the field." Were you aware -- first of all, were you aware of that order at the time, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw it for the first time on the 25th of January, in the hotel, when I saw the other documentation brought to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you understand that an order of that type would be issued?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything disputable about it. The commander of the Military District agreed to carry out as much as ordered, and, in fact, confirms my order by issuing the order to disengage from combat MP units; and this order is directed down his chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And does your order of August 9th represent any interference with General Gotovina's authority over the military police, pursuant to Article 9?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did General Gotovina continue to have authority over -- were the military police units, did they remain subordinate to him, pursuant to Article 9, at least those military units within the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am loathe to get on my feet, Mr. President. The confusion that is being here by the questions now, I'm afraid, is heading us into a train wreck. The terminology -- if we can refer to what was withdrawn in paragraph 1 and ask him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, I think you would meet some of the concerns of Mr. Misetic by sticking closer to the text and to identify exactly what you are referring to. And I have one -- let me just see ... Yes, apparently the literally text is of great concern to Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, I apologise, Mr. President. What I meant was we're talking about this order, and this order refers to specific military police units being withdrawn and -- the witness, I believe, will be able to explain it further. But then the question got broadened out to say, Does he still have command over the military police under Article 9 which is a more general question than what we're talking about with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you be specific, but perhaps after the break. And I have one question for you, Mr. Tieger. You referred to "your order of August the 9th," which is a report with requests and suggestions, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We looked at two items, two documents from August 9th. The first was the report with the recommendations, which was sent to Minister Susak, and so on. The second was the -- is D837 an order by Mr. Lausic of the same date. And I hope that clarifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just so I don't leave it, there was a suggestion that I reconfigure the question about the last matter that was raised. I looked at the transcript. In the interests of time and efficiency, I think I'm inclined to move on. I just wanted to indicate -- didn't want to leave things hanging. If the Court thought something needed to be clarified, but I though -- I looked at the record and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we turn next please to P877.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, P877 is an order issued by you on the 18th of August, 1995. The subject was "Full implementation of military police tasks in liberated territory, efficient cooperation with the MUP, and an order." And it begins: "The military police administration received an official letter from the MUP of the Republic of Croatia on 17 of August, 1995, stating that in the territory of the Republic of Croatia that was liberated during the Operation Storm, there are still daily instances of houses being burned, of looting of moveable property, as well as other forms of illegal behaviour committed by the HV members and civilians wearing the HV uniforms." It goes on to note that cooperation between the military police and the civilian police, according to the official letter, has not yielded results thus far, in accordance with the basic premises of the state policy and that this cooperation should, therefore, be removed. It indicates that the Ministry of Internal Affairs had received several complaints from foreign ambassadors, drawing attention to the behaviour of the HV members and stressing the need to eliminate such instances. And then you go on to issue an order that commanders of military police platoon, companies, and battalions, are ... to contact immediately the chiefs of police stations and heads of police administrations in this area and have a meeting, in order to analyse the security situation and so forth. Number 2: Commanders of military police platoons, companies and battalions are to contact immediately the highest-ranking HV commander in their areas of responsibility and completely implement item 6 of the military police administration order giving a number, dating 16th of August, 1995. And this order is sent, of course, to the military police battalion as indicated on the front page, and also delivered to the Main Staff, the assistant minister for security, to the assistant minister for the MUP, and to the commanders of the Military Districts. Now, the order refers to an official letter from the Ministry of Interior the day before your order, referring to the daily instances of burning of houses, looting of movable property committed by HV members and civilians. Had you been aware of the continuing problem of burning and looting by HV members before the time you were advised of that -- of those events in an official letter from Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer to your question is contained in the daily reports sent to the highest levels of the Ministry of Interior and Main Staff. Therein, I stress the problem of unlawful and undisciplined behaviour of HV members. I also put forward certain suggestions and requests. Specifically, in terms of this order, it is true that the day before, on the 17th of August, I personally received a letter from the MUP assistant minister, Mr. Josko Moric, in which he stressed the problem of arson, unlawful taking away of property, and the other things you mentioned. But virtue of this order of mine, which I based on my previous orders, and we have them stipulated therein, referring to the 14th of August, the 5th of August, the 16th of August, I asked for the establishment of a better, more effective and daily cooperation with the civilian police at all levels from the lowest level; that is, platoons, to the highest level; that is to say, the battalions. And I asked for daily joint meetings and that notes be kept and then forwarded to the military police administration, so that we, at the highest level, could meet with those in charge of the civilian police, in order to assess the crisis points and intervene along our respective lines of work. Our colleagues from the MUP were supposed to address those issues within their ministry, and, we, in turn, in ours. In this order, mention is made that there is a need to establish contact immediately with the chiefs of the police stations and police administrations and that at meetings held with them, the security situation should be analysed and that specific and efficient models of cooperation should be set up when acting independently and jointly. In item 2, I state that the commanders of platoons, companies, and battalions, are immediately to contact the -- most senior HV commander in their areas of responsibility and to implement item 6 of the order of the 16th of August. I also state that in that order, in item 6, I had ordered the commanders of HV military police units to get acquainted with the deployment of HV units along the front lines as well as the deployment of HV units in camps, the staffing numbers of the units and access of activity or when leaving the area of responsibility. They were also supposed to get the numbers of those in charge of various HV units and to exchange numbers with them. I wanted them to get fully acquainted with their respective AORs, based on which they were to determine the deployment of their MP patrols. I toured the field in person, especially in Banja, Kordun, and Lika; and my deputy toured the area towards Dalmatia, whereby we realised that the commanders of certain HV units, of reserve brigades, and some other smaller units were changing their camp locations, setting up temporary camps at certain locations without notifying the military police units concerned; and those military police units were not able to get by that information at a higher level. They simply had no overview of their respective territories. That's why I ordered that they should study their areas of responsibility, in terms of HV troops to establish contact with those units, exchange phone numbers, in order to set up efficient contact so that they could adequately dispatch their patrols and staff, so that we wouldn't have a situation in which a -- a MP patrol would be in an area where there are no HV troops at all, and, on the other hand, to avoid having situations in which there were HV troops in certain areas without a single military policemen present. And just to sum up in two sentences: I wanted to say that it was at that time we decided to change your tactics and method which, until that point was based on check-points, where jointly with the civilian police, we controlled entry and exit to the newly liberated territory. That method proved inefficient, because both the civilian population entering the area as well as HV members, and others, who wore HV uniforms whether being HV troops or not, used other traffic routes. Of course, there were casualties along such routes because many of them were mined. We also took note of that and kept records, and we concluded that the model, based on check-points, was lacking; that we were supposed to enter the area, act preventively, and possibly catch the perpetrators in action. In simple words, that would mean being present trying to prevent things from happening rather than waiting at check-points, particularly because people knew where check-points were and used alternative routes to take away the booty. Most of those were inhabitants, were native to the liberated region. They knew it very well and that was a thing that hindered our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I want to turn --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to seek some clarification of one of your answers. Mr. Tieger asked you whether you had been aware of this continuing problem even before you were advised of that in the official letter from Mr. Moric. Then you said: "I think the answer to your question is contained in the daily reports sent to the highest levels of the Ministry of Interior and Main Staff. Therein, I stress the problem of unlawful and undisciplined behaviour of HV members." May I take it from this answer that when you are referring to unlawful and undisciplined behaviour, that you had looting and burning on your mind? Not exclusively perhaps, but including looting and burning of houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is absolutely correct. I just wanted to make a small correction, and I apologise for it, but not to the highest level of the Ministry of Interior but to the highest level of the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then as a co-product of the question, there a correction on the transcript. Mr. Tieger, I thought you were quoting literally from that letter, isn't it? But if that's the case, you're using a document which is not the same as what appears on my screen. I just mention one matter. You, I think, twice, once when reading, but later also you referred to an official letter whereas the document on my screen talks about the communication. Could we perhaps check that, because if it is not the same document, there may be other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, you are correct. I notice the same thing. I think Mr. Tieger may be using a draft, or the draft is in e-court, one or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have to verify that so that we have the -- there appear to be two translations one from which you read, Mr. Tieger, and one which was on our screen. And I'm not insisting on having it resolved immediately. But could you please verify that and resolve that matter? Just if I read from the screen, I read that: "The military police administration received a communication from the Republic of Croatia MUP on the 17th of August, 1995, stating that in the area of the Republic of Croatia liberated in the course of Operation Storm, houses are being torched." And there, in your reading, you already went to the daily occurrence more or less of those events, which in my version only comes at the end of this sentence. I didn't notice any major discrepancies although a communication and an official letter, well, could be the same. But could we please verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, and thank you. No question those are two different translations, and I'll -- sounds like I'm not using the one that is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I want to turn to a document issued at approximately the same time. That's D49. And that's a document from Mr. Moric at the Ministry of Interior to various police administrations on the 18th of August, 1995. Now, Mr. Moric refers, in the first paragraph, to reports concerning torching of houses and illegal taking away of movable property in the areas liberated in Operation Storm. He says: "Most of these acts are perpetrated by individuals wearing Croatian army uniforms. The facts indicate that these individuals are, formally and actually, members of the Croatian army, but there are also individuals who are not members of the Croatian army, but are wrongfully wearing Croatian army uniforms." And then he notes: "The torching of houses and illegal taking away of people's movable property has assumed such proportions that it is inflicting political damage on the Republic of Croatia, both at home and abroad." And so he issues the following order: The first point of the order is that police administration chiefs must immediately convene a meeting with the commanders of military police battalions to inform them of the problem and of the decision to put a stop to it. The second point is that: "The meeting must be informed of the decision that cases of torching of houses and illegal taking away of people's movable property that have hitherto occurred will not be operatively investigated, but a stop must be put to cases of this type as of today." The third point of his order is the request to commanders military police battalion for mixed barrier check-points and mixed patrols of civilian and military police to be set up in all populated areas where there are members of the HV. And the fourth point concerns an agreement that Mr. Moric, Assistant Minister Moric says that: "It is should be agreed that as of today, an on-site investigation and forensic and operative criminal processing will be conducted after every case of torching of houses and illegal taking away of people's movable property." Now, first, Mr. Lausic, I wanted to know if you were aware of this order or about the time or about the time it was issued by Assistant Minister Moric?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right after I received the aforementioned letter, I received from Mr. Josko Moric on the 18th of August, I got in touch with him over the phone. We agreed that I should regulate matters by virtue of my order to the military police units, in order to improve cooperation with the civilian police, and that Mr. Moric, as assistant minister, would issue a separate instruction in the form we see before us and send it to the heads of police administrations and police stations. I don't have this document in my documentation, and I did not come across it in the MP archives, although I was included on the list. However, I cannot confirm that I was familiar with this document before that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do I understand correctly that after you received the letter from Assistant Minister Moric that was dated 17th of August, that prompted your order, you spoke with him about the problems raised in that 17 August letter; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I received his letter on the 17th of August, I called him by phone immediately. I told him I had received his letter, and I suggested that we act in our respective areas - that is to say, I was to address the MP units and he -- the civilian police units -- in order to ensure that, on a daily basis, they have efficient exchange of information and joint tactics and methods, as well as the way of reporting. The result of that telephone conversation was my order of the 18th of August, and on his part, he issued the document which I was unable to locate in the military police archives, and I don't have it in my documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: His order says that when the police administration chiefs meet with the commanders of military police battalions to inform them of the problem and of the decision to put a stop to it, the meeting, which I understand to be the meeting between the police administration chiefs and the military police battalion commanders must be informed of the decision that cases of torching of houses and illegal taking away of people's movable property that have hitherto occurred, or already occurred, will not be operatively investigated. Who made that decision; if you know?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that for the first time in Mr. Moric's letter. I was not familiar with that previously. It is he who issued this document to his subordinate chiefs of police administrations and not -- it was not sent to the military police. Perhaps we can go back to the front page to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I don't think there is any indication in the document that it was sent to the military police. Did you and Mr. Moric discuss during your conversation before you issued your order of August 18th that -- the possibility of deciding or of a decision to refrain from investigating cases of burning and looting that are already occurred, or that had occurred up to that point?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The telephone conversation was a short one, and to interpret it liberally in the following way: Josko, I received your memo and my situation is that you take your vertical chain of command. I should take mine and inform our chiefs of administration to meet up and see the best ways of preventing such incidents. And the methods that they would use and how to best put to use the resources human and otherwise to deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you receive information from any of your military police battalion commanders that police administration chiefs or other minister of interior officials were not collaborating in or not getting involved in the investigation of cases of looting and burning that had taken place up to August 18th?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know the extent to which the Ministry of Interior was collaborating with or cooperating with any military police efforts to investigate cases of looting and burning that had taken place up to August 18th?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cooperation aimed at preventing incidents and employing repressive measures differed from area to area, unit to unit. At any rate, both from the military police side and the civilian police side, the efforts focussed on preventing the unlawful conduct, and arresting the perpetrators and punishing them. I didn't have information from either my commanders or from other levels for that matter, that an order was issued from some quarter that -- that certain cases should not be processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Item 3 of the Moric order provides that the commanders of military police battalions are to be requested that mixed barrier check-points and mixed patrols of civilian and military police be set up in all populated areas where there are members of the Croatian army; and that the task of those check-points and patrols will be to prevent the aforementioned problems. Now, that -- that would seem to indicate that, up to that point, mixed barrier check-points and mixed patrols of civilian and military police had not been set up in all populated areas where there were members of the Croatian army. Do you not the extent to which such mixed barrier check-points and mixed patrols had been established and pursued by the 18th of August?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you any precise data. It could most probably be found in the MUP archives or the MP -- or, rather, the MP archives or the MP documentation you have. I can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention, then, to another document that reflects events approximately one month later. Let's turn to your diary, Mr. Lausic, that's 65 ter 1880, at pages 68 through 71 of the English, and 62 through 64 of the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And to keep the record as clear as possible, I'm helpfully advised that is now P2166, rather than 65 ter 1880.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And specifically, Mr. Lausic, I'm looking at an entry from your diary of 15 September, 1995. And it reflects a meeting at 1100 hours, a coordination meeting of the MUP and the military police attended by among others, Mr. Moric, Mr. Benko, Brigadier Biskic, Colonel Kozic, Major Juric, Captain Eljuga, and various commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, just for the record, 65 ter 1880 is now P2166. The list has been distributed. The documents were admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought I mentioned that specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. No, I apologise. I really apologise, Mr. Tieger. I'm doing things that I sometimes blame other people for doing. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am confident the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I wanted to bring your attention to certain portions of your diary entry from September 15th and ask you some questions about that. First of all, we see the comments of Mr. Matic, the second -- apparently the second speaker, who indicates that the -- in the third comment list there that the military police is present only at two check-points out of a total of 11. Do you recall whether that was an accurate reflection, generally, of the extent to which the establishment of joint check-points was successful or unsuccessful, after the -- after your conversation with Mr. Moric on August 18th, and after the respective orders issued by you and Mr. Moric on that date?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, my notes that we can see here are certainly authentic. Now, as to what sort of situation prevailed in different areas, this cannot be portrayed merely on the basis of what Mr. Matic, chief of the Sibenik police administration, had to say. Other chiefs of police administrations conclude here that the situation was satisfactory. At any rate, the presence of the military policemen in certain areas was the crucial problem. That's to say, how to best put to use the number of policemen that we had, whether to keep them on the check-points or send them out on to patrols in order to be widely present in the area and catch perpetrators red-handed, et cetera. This is something that we can talk about in general terms. However without having specific numbers and specific steps taken, one should not make any conclusions merely on the basis of what Mr. Matic, chief of the Sibenik police administration, had to say; namely that out of the 11 check-points, only two were also manned by the military police. In the context of his statement, I will take the liberty of quoting the remainder of what he says and that's something that I noted: "The general public law and order is satisfactory, 150 perpetrators were caught. 19 of which were members of the HV. Out of 11 only -- only 2 check-points are also covered by the military police. The check-points are being bypassed as they are many side roads. These side roads are mined. Meaning that those who try to avoid the check-points by taking the side roads enter into minefields and get killed. Cooperation with the military police is excellent, but the problem is the lack of personnel on the side of the military police. The many motor vehicles in circulation without licence plates constitute a problem." So this is the entirety of what he to say. The isolated statement where he said that the military police was present at two check-points out of a total of 11 does not portray the full picture of the situation as reflected in what he had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's why I precisely why I asked you about it. Can I turn to Mr. Cetina, the chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration. Mr. Cetina said: "Significant problems in the field with looting and burning of houses and property in the newly liberated areas." Was that diary entry an accurate reflection of what Mr. Cetina said?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise I should like to present all of the entries I made as having been said by the chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration, Mr. Cetina. First bullet points: Significant problems in the field with looting and burning of houses and property in the newly liberated areas, burning of haystacks, and killing of livestock. Criminal investigation is underway to individual the perpetrators of these crimes. The problem lies in the fact that the offenders bypass the check-points and circulate along the side roads. There has been cooperation with the military police but not to such an extent that the responsibility reached down to the lowest levels. Shortage of military police personnel is also a problem. There were many problems with certificates issued by civilian authorities. Mayors of municipalities authorising the appropriation of assets and various property.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, prior to this meeting of September 15th, 1995, had you been aware of the significant problems in the field with looting and burning of houses and property in the Zadar-Knin police administration area?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the documentation, you will find an entry from my diary dated the 13th of September, that's to say two days before the Plitvice meeting, where, at 10.00 in the Ministry of Interior, a coordinating meeting at the highest level was held between the civilian and military police forces. Assistant Minister Moric, chiefs of the police sector, traffic police, then Assistant Minister Benko for the crime police were there on behalf of the MUP; whereas I was there, my deputy was there, and the chiefs of the general duty traffic and crime MP were there on behalf of the MOD. At that meeting, on the 13th, the colleagues from the MUP advanced their comments an observations which I made note of in my diary according to which the military policemen at the check-points were quite flexible and did not, to the full extent, apply powers; that patrols were not observed moving along roads; that there was shortage of policemen; that generally speaking everyone was in full cooperation; but that the military police commanders justified themselves by the lack of personnel; that there were no problems with professional units but that there were many problems with Home Guard units; that there were many vehicles without licence plates cruising around, et cetera, et cetera. Then you have Mr. Moric speaking next.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And at the end of the meeting, it was agreed, or, rather, the conclusions from the meeting of the 13th of September were that on the 15th of September a coordinating meeting should be held at Plitvice where I was supposed to call all the MP battalion commanders that Mr. Moric would be calling all the chiefs of police administrations to be present there; in order for all of them to present the problems and the suggestions for the cooperation and the sort of cooperation to be set up based on the human and materiel resources we had; in order to coordinate the use of the human and materiel resources present in the area to coordinate our activities and to carry out joint activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Since you have referred us to that September 13th meeting, and that can be found at --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it still the case for the Registrar that ERN numbers are best for locating the document? Okay. Then the September 15th -- September 13th meeting, excuse me. Let me try this one more way. I'm sorry. I was on the 15th meeting which we had in front of us before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn, if I may, Mr. Lausic, to your comments at that meeting, the coordination meeting which you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's found at page 70 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic you stated there that: "Looting, killing and burning of houses continue, and the perpetrators come from all structures." Now when you say the perpetrators came -- come from all structures, can you explain to the Court what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problems both we and the civilian police were faced with was that the liberated area was being entered into by the civilians who had been driven out of the area through the Serb occupation and had in the meantime been accommodated at various locations. As soon as the area was liberated, they moved into the region to see the condition their property was in and what the situation was like in general. Members of the Home Guard Regiments also went into the area although the combat activities had ceased, and their presence there was no longer required. However, let me remind you, that members of the Home Guard Regiments were mostly made up of the local population that had been mobilised into those ranks. In addition to that, there were masses of people from other areas wearing HV uniforms, although not members of the HV. They included -- or, rather, all the individuals I mentioned now covered, I guess, all of these various structures though there were many other situations involving other types of people, and it would take a lot of time for me to explain them all or describe them all here. Another problem was that, as early as the 7th of August, the highest-ranking officials of the Republic of Croatia had proclaimed that area to be an area where the civilian authorities became fully operational, which made it impossible to seal off the entire area and enforce strict control over the movement into and out of the area. Another problem was that the demobilisation process of the reserve forces of the HV which had been mobilised prior to Operation Storm, was very slow until the 12th of August, when several tens of thousands of troops were supposed to be demobilised in the Split area. By the 12th of August, only 5.000 were demobilised. There was a social aspect to that. The demobilised members of the Home Guard Regiments did not have a civilian life to go back to. They didn't have jobs to go back to, didn't have homes to go back to, and their life, under the garb of the HV uniform, in the garb of the HV uniform was the key solution to all their problems in their life. This was something that made the work of the civilian and military police equally difficult because you had individuals present in the area, wearing the HV uniform, some of whom were not HV members. There were many other problems in that area as well. One had to make sure that one knew that the membership of the HV could not be attested to by ones wearing a uniform but rather by ones producing the HV identification papers. There were many aggravating circumstances that made the work of the military police difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your penultimate entry in your diary, referring to your comments on that date, states: "Bring the line of command into the problem. Commanders at all levels must be aware of the problem and must resolve issues following the line of command." Was that one of the circumstances that made the work of the military police difficult?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, that's correct. My insisting on having the line or chain of command organised in such a way to facilitate the work of the military police. My insistence on having the military policemen adhere to all the relevant rules, all of that was supposed to prevent any such occurrences. The constant -- this is the constant thread that permeates all my orders and documents I issued. One has to comprehend the priorities of these commanders who were, at the same time, displaced persons and individuals who to a great extent did not have the power or the clout to keep their men under their command. And, in many cases, they lost the power over their men because their men were, in turn, displaced persons whose homes had been burned. It was very difficult for them to contain their excessive behaviour. My note that I -- that one needs to keep under control the chain of command, that commanders at all levels must be aware of the problem and must resolve issues following the chain of command, this is something that you will see in all documents that I produced relating to Operation Storm. I will take the liberty of using an another rhetorical figure of speech. And I said, Woe betide the commander whose men must be disciplined by the military police; and woe betide the father whose child must be disciplined by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I see your eyes on the clock and this is an appropriate time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just, for housekeeping purposes if we could figure out how we're going to schedule things because we have another witness next week, and I'm not sure, depending on the timing, whether we are going to be able to get to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we do that in the absence of the witness. Mr. Lausic, I'd like to instruct you as I did yesterday that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony whether already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow in the afternoon in this same courtroom, at quarter past 2.00. Could you follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My predictive abilities are not overly precise. I certainly would attempt to use no more than the first session tomorrow, but I find that matters move sometimes often slower, sometimes faster than I might have predicted. So I would ask the Court's indulgence. I think can you see I have moved over certain areas fairly quickly with efficiency and expediency in mind; and I will continue to do so, but that continues to be a bit of a problem. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, right now, I would estimate about nine sessions given, I think, we have about 250 documents from OTP that are either coming as bar table or through the witness, if I'm not mistaken. And I'm hopeful that that nine includes the fact that I hope to speed him up and shorten some of his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I will be after Mr. Misetic. It depends very much what he covers, and we will be logging those areas as he covers them to take passages out of our planned cross-examination. I anticipate he will cover certain areas thoroughly. And, therefore, it looks to me like could I deal with my cross-examination in a day. I don't want to be held to that if Mr. Misetic doesn't cover those areas as I'm sure the Court would understand, as this is a highly important witness for all parties in the case and the Court and important that matters are covered thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, it very much depends on the work of my predecessors, but I don't estimate to have more than one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That depends -- of course, sometimes the answers of the witness are detailed, and I'm not always convinced that it is the level of detail sought by the one who puts the question to the witness. I would like everyone to keep this in mind and to intervene where an answer goes in the direction which is -- I would not say a different direction, but at least not exactly what the party is aiming at. That might save quite some time. That's -- Then before we adjourn, I was inaccurate this morning when I spoke about the admission into evidence of three documents of the list yesterday. What actually happened is that 65 ter 2978 was taken from the list because it was already included in 65 ter 1880, which has now become P2166. The other two 65 ter numbers I referred to earlier today were not admitted yesterday but were admitted into evidence as P1216 and P1211. We adjourn, and we will resume tomorrow, the 28th of January, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of January, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
